facts.claim: Silica microspheres act as contact optical elements in an ordinary white-light microscope; actual targets are fabricated inorganic/optical-storage structures.
The source states sphere refractive index 1.46 and recommends a practical diameter interval strictly between 2 and 9 micrometers.

The explicitly identified grating, AAO and Blu-ray examples use 4.74 micrometer spheres; an additional successful 3.0 micrometer size is reported. The associated star-panel text/caption does not separately state its sphere diameter.

Commercial colloidal silica spheres came from Bangs Laboratories; a diluted suspension was drop-coated onto the target and formed an ordered monolayer through self-assembly. Solvent, concentration, volume, drying program and lot are not supplied.
The reported optical platform is Olympus MX-850 with an Olympus MDPlan 80x objective of numerical aperture 0.9. A halogen lamp peaking near 600 nm supplied white light.
The transmission grating comprises 360 nm wide lines with 130 nm gaps in a 30 nm chrome coating on fused silica. Fabrication used a Quanta 200 3D focused-ion-beam instrument.
For that grating, the reported virtual plane lies 2.5 micrometers below the substrate surface and magnification is 4.17x. Features outside sphere-covered areas were unresolved.

The transmission fishnet target has gold on anodic aluminum oxide; the source gives 50 nm pore diameter and 50 nm spacing, an AAO template thickness of 300 micrometers and a gold film thickness of 20 nm.
Two-stage anodization and template-based formation of the porous gold film are reported preparation stages. The source provides only partial preparation details.
facts.evidence_class: reported preparation identity; hazardous operating recipe intentionally excluded

facts.claim: The AAO example reports about 8x magnification and a 400 nm image-plane separation associated with the 50 nm object feature. Gold is described as improving resolution and magnification relative to the uncoated condition, without a paired uncoated figure/data series.
The reflection track sample is a commercial Blu-ray optical disc. A 100 micrometer transparent protective layer was removed. Body and SEM labels give 200 nm lines with 100 nm gaps.
A star-shaped pattern on an optical-disc phase-change thin film was imaged in reflection; the source claims 90 nm corner detail. Body calls the film SbTe, while Fig3b caption says GeSbTe.

The star-pattern preparation is attributed to a contact particle lens array method described in reference 20, an earlier laser-patterning paper. The current source does not supply its complete fabrication recipe.
facts.source_location: MAIN p5, sample preparation and reference 20

facts.claim: All reported SEM images used a Hitachi S-3400N. SEM provides feature-size/reference morphology comparisons to optical images, not a stated traceable calibration chain.
Experimental fused-silica half-ball SIL controls from Edmund Optics have diameters 0.5 mm and 2.5 mm. The smaller used an 80x objective and the larger a 40x objective because of physical clearance.
Bare target, 0.5 mm SIL, 2.5 mm SIL and 4.74 micrometer sphere conditions are displayed for the Blu-ray target. Only the sphere condition resolves the track pattern in the reported example.
Authors state both SILs failed across all target types with 50-130 nm features. Those non-Blu-ray controls are not shown individually.

Ten- and fifty-micrometer spheres failed reported 100 nm imaging tests. One-micrometer spheres were unsuccessful because their view windows were too small; that lower limitation is explicitly practical, not a theoretical impossibility.

Three-micrometer spheres are reported to yield 50 nm images; 4.74 micrometer spheres are reported to magnify about 1.2 times as much as 3.0 micrometer spheres. No replicate counts or uncertainty are supplied.
Authors claim complex structures can also be imaged in transmission and that both modes reach 50 nm. No corresponding 50 nm reflection or complex-shape transmission panel is supplied.

Source theoretical work includes Mie analysis of sphere size/index, FDTD comparisons of SIL/sphere/particle-on-surface, geometrical ray tracing in Mathematica 7.0, and a Fortran Mie/Poynting-flow calculation.
facts.evidence_class: reported numerical/theoretical method; not run here

facts.claim: The Fig4 particle-on-surface calculation uses a 40 nm gold film, sphere radius 2.37 micrometers, index 1.46 and wavelength 600 nm. Displayed peak intensities are 90, 107 and 153 for SIL, sphere and particle-on-surface, respectively. These are model outputs, not detector readings.

A geometrical-optics-based field-enhancement heuristic has exponent about 0.34; the source says it differs from the geometrical-optics comparison by less than 1 percent for index 1-1.95. Its particle-on-surface estimate is about 5.5x.
facts.evidence_class: reported approximation, not a validated experimental transfer model

facts.claim: Poynting-line extrapolation yields a 2-4x virtual magnification depending on the selected line, separate from the roughly 5.5x heuristic and measured 4-8x examples.
A high-index optimum near 1.8, possible larger spheres and sub-20 nm imaging are predictive extrapolations, not experimentally demonstrated branches of this paper.

No replicate/sample counts, uncertainty budgets, predefined quantitative experimental image-resolution acceptance criterion, camera specification, measurement calibration certificate, raw-data repository or detailed closeout protocol is supplied in the inspected main/SI.

The paper shows multiple sphere-covered regions and discusses combining the corresponding views into a larger image; no complete stitching method, calibrated mosaic, error map or throughput result is supplied.
facts.evidence_class: illustrated array coverage plus proposed image combination

safe_scope: No biological specimens, cultivation, engineering, viral work or molecular protocol is proposed. Future biological applications in the source are excluded.
